newsitem.title: UK: Drop in UK grind due to halt at Mars butter plant.
newsitem.headline: Drop in UK grind due to halt at Mars butter plant.

text.p: A drop in the UK's fourth quarter cocoa grind was due to a temporary slowdown at one of Mars's processing plants but the year's underlying consumption remained exceptionally strong, industry and trader sources said.

The Biscuit, Cake, Chocolate and Confectionery Alliance (BCCCA) said on Thursday fourth quarter grindings had dropped 3.3 percent to 45,147 tonnes from the same quarter of 1995 versus forecasts of a five percent decline.
But due to large increases in previous quarters, partly triggered by resumption of idle capacity, the cumulative grind for 1996 was still 18.5 percent above 1995 at 189,037 tonnes.
"The market has expanded quite well, but it's not always reflected in the grind," said one industry representative.

Market sources said the leading UK confectionery manufacturer Mars had slowed processing at its cocoa butter plant in Selby, Yorkshire, possibly due to overgrinding the year before which could have produced excess stocks.

"That plant runs pretty fast. It's understandable that they put it on and off," said another industry representative, adding that the powerful Selby plant could make a difference of 5-10 percent to the total UK grind.
The UK data followed European final quarter grind figures this week which were largely within expectations.
One exception was the German grind which was sharply down by 21.2 percent to 56,254 tonnes but this was mainly due to changes in processing capacity at Hamester.
The Dutch quarter grind rose 3.90 percent to 97,273 tonnes.
"If you put the Dutch and the German grind together, the year-on-year increase is four percent which is not surprising," said one trader.
The UK grind came days after a review by Cadbury and its sweet-making arm Trebor Bassett concluded that British confectioney sales grew by five percent last year to a record stg 4.9 billion.
Volume sales in Britain rose by two percent last year to 833,000 tonnes, marking an increase of more than 12 percent over the last decade, said the Confectionery Market Review.
"The question is how fast it will grow rather than any risk it will not grow," it said.
